claim: Humans can judge whether a wall is stable or collapsing in a fraction of a second.
source: We, wise or not, can easily judge whether a wall is stable or collapsing in a fraction of a second (Battaglia et al., 2013; Kubricht et al., 2017; McCloskey, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Battaglia et al., 2013; Kubricht et al., 2017; McCloskey, 1983)

claim: Humans can report the stability of a 10-block stack with a satisfactory accuracy of 70% on average.
source: Taking a stack consisting of 10 blocks as an example (Figure 1), we can quickly report its stability with a satisfactory accuracy of 70% on average (Bear et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Bear et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2016)

claim: The universal cardinality of possible configurations for a 10-block stack is at least 1.14 × 10^50.
source: but the universal cardinality of possible configurations is at least 1.14 × 1050 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is much larger than the total number of sand grains on Earth (est. 7.5 × 1018) (Blatner, 2013).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation (Blatner, 2013)

claim: 4-month-old infants expect a box to fall if it loses contact with a support platform.
source: Contrary to this intuition, 4-month-old infants, who have little visual experience of the physical world, expect a box to fall if it loses contact with a support platform (Baillargeon, 2004; Baillargeon, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Baillargeon, 2004; Baillargeon, 1994)

claim: Infants as young as 7 months expect a downward-moving object to accelerate and an upward-moving object to decelerate.
source: For example, infants as young as 7 months expect a downward-moving object to accelerate and an upward-moving object to decelerate (Friedman, 2002; Kim and Spelke, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Friedman, 2002; Kim and Spelke, 1999)

claim: Adults can estimate the remaining time to catch a moving ball.
source: and adults can estimate the remaining time to catch a moving ball (McIntyre et al., 2001; Zago and Lacquaniti, 2005) even in the absence of visual information (Lacquaniti and Maioli, 1989; Zago et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (McIntyre et al., 2001; Zago and Lacquaniti, 2005; Lacquaniti and Maioli, 1989; Zago et al., 2009)

claim: The parieto-insular vestibular cortex in the brain is the neural basis for gravity-based stability inference.
source: Further fMRI studies have revealed the parieto-insular vestibular cortex in the brain as the neural basis for gravity-based stability inference, suggesting that this knowledge is encapsulated as a cognitive module (Fischer et al., 2016; Indovina et al., 2005; Pramod et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to fMRI studies (Fischer et al., 2016; Indovina et al., 2005; Pramod et al., 2022)

claim: Participants were 91.0% accurate in reporting collapse trajectories as normal when θ equals 0.
source: As expected, when θ is equal to 0 (i.e., the direction of the simulated gravity is the direction of the natural gravity), the participants were likely to report that the collapse trajectory was normal (accuracy: 91.0%, STD: 8.0%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: The confidence level of reporting normal trajectories decreased gradually as a function of θ and was best fit by a Gaussian function with σ=19.9.
source: Contrary to this intuition, the subjective sense of the abnormality was not immediately apparent as θ moved away from 0; instead, the confidence level of reporting normal trajectories decreased gradually as a function of θ, which was the best fit by a Gaussian function with σ=19.9 (Figure 1d, left).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 1d

claim: Participants were 50.9% confident in reporting a normal collapse trajectory when the vertical offset of θ was 19.9°.
source: That is, the participants were 50.9% confident in reporting a normal collapse trajectory when the vertical offset of θ was 19.9°.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Accuracy in detecting the abnormality was not affected by φ.
source: In addition, accuracy in detecting the abnormality was not affected by φ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), consistent with the uniformly distributed gravitational field in the physical world.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The world model on gravity encodes gravity's direction as a Gaussian distribution with the vertical direction as the maximum likelihood.
source: Therefore, the world model on gravity is unlikely to be a faithful replica of the physical world; instead, it encodes gravity's direction as a Gaussian distribution with the vertical direction as the maximum likelihood (Figure 1d, right).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results shown in Figure 1d

claim: Each participant's σ in the upright condition was in high agreement with the σ in the upside-down condition (r = 0.91, p<0.01).
source: Indeed, each participant's σ in the upright condition was in high agreement with the σ in the upside-down condition (r = 0.91, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The visual experience and task context did not cognitively penetrate humans' world model on gravity.
source: That is, the visual experience and task context apparently did not cognitively penetrate humans' world model on gravity, suggesting that it is likely encapsulated as a cognitive module.
evidence: Inferred from the consistency of σ values across different experimental conditions

claim: NGS-estimated stability was significantly correlated with participants' subjective sense (r = 0.70, p<0.01).
source: NGS-estimated stability was significantly correlated with participants' subjective sense (Figure 2b, bottom; r = 0.70, p<0.01), consistent with previous findings (Battaglia et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and citation to previous research

claim: Participants showed an obvious bias towards predicting a collapse for stacks regardless of their actual stability (inference bias = –0.31, p<0.01).
source: However, the participants showed an obvious bias towards predicting a collapse for stacks regardless of their actual stability, as the dots in Figure 2b are more concentrated on the lower side of the diagonal line. This phenomenon is referred to as the inference bias, which was indexed as the difference in stability estimates between the participants and the NGS (inference bias = –0.31, p<0.01; see 'Methods').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The MGS showed a similar magnitude of correlation in stability estimates with participants (r = 0.75, p<0.01).
source: Aside from a similar magnitude of the correlation in the stability estimates between the participants and the MGS (Figure 2c, bottom; r = 0.75, p<0.01)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c

claim: The MGS more precisely reflected participants' judgments of stability with an inference bias of 0.04 (p>0.05).
source: the MGS, in contrast to the NGS, more precisely reflected participants' judgments of stability because the points were evenly distributed along the diagonal line (inference bias = 0.04, p>0.05; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for the agreement when the MGS was implemented with different Gaussian functions).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The MGS found stacks of all heights to be more prone to collapse (inference bias <0, p<0.01 for all heights).
source: Consistent with the inference bias found in humans, the MGS found stacks of all heights to be more prone to collapse (Figure 2d, right; inference bias <0, p<0.01 for all heights).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2d

claim: The inference bias increased monotonically with increasing height.
source: Critically, the bias increased monotonically with increasing height, consistent with the illusion that taller objects are considered more prone to collapse (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for the inference bias when the MGS was equipped with different levels of deviation).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The distribution of updated probabilities in the direction space was gradational (σ = 21.6) after reinforcement learning training.
source: Although gravity's direction in the environment was vertical, the distribution of updated probabilities in the direction space was gradational (σ = 21.6; Figure 3b, right), which is close to gravity's direction represented in the world model derived from the psychophysics experiment on human participants.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3b

claim: All world models trained with different numbers of blocks represented gravity's direction in a Gaussian distribution.
source: We trained the world model on gravity under the same RL framework for each world and found that all world models represented gravity's direction in a Gaussian distribution (Figure 3c, left; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for all world models).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The width of the Gaussian distribution (σ) decreased monotonically as the number of blocks increased.
source: However, the width of the distribution, indexed by the parameter of σ, decreased monotonically as the number of blocks increased (Figure 3c, right).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3c

claim: The accuracy at the plateau for the NGS was close to 100% (95.3% on average), significantly higher than that for the MGS (80.1% on average) (t = 19.59, p<0.001).
source: As expected, for the NGS (i.e., the world model with the deterministic direction of gravity), the accuracy at the plateau was close to 100% (95.3% on average, Figure 4b, top red box), significantly higher than that for the MGS (80.1% on average, Figure 4b, top blue box) (t = 19.59, p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 4b

claim: The MGS reached the plateau crucial for decision-making sooner than the NGS (response time: 27.1% vs 75.2%, t = 15.58, p<0.001).
source: However, while the initial growth rates of both models were comparable, the MGS reached the plateau crucial for decision-making sooner than the NGS (response time, indexed by the ratio between the time to reach the plateau and the time to reach the final stage: 27.1% vs 75.2%, t = 15.58, p<0.001) (Figure 4b middle).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 4b

claim: The stochastic world model provided a better balance between accuracy and speed, with an efficiency significantly higher than that provided by the NGS (3.49 vs 1.32, t = 9.12, p<0.001).
source: In addition, by integrating the prediction accuracy and the response time as a measure of efficiency, we found that the stochastic world model provided a better balance between accuracy and speed, with an efficiency significantly higher than that provided by the NGS (3.49 vs 1.32, t = 9.12, p<0.001; Figure 4b, bottom).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 4b

claim: The variance of humans' inference on stability best matched that of the MGS after three simulations.
source: We found that the variance of humans' inference on stability best matched that of the MGS after three simulations (Figure 4d; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for the model-behavior correspondence under different numbers of simulations).
evidence: Supported by comparison between human data and computational modeling shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Humans are likely to run simulations a limited number of times to infer stacks' stability.
source: Therefore, humans are likely to run simulations a limited number of times to infer stacks' stability.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that human variance matches MGS with three simulations

claim: The world model on gravity is not a faithful replica of the physical laws, but instead encoded gravity's vertical direction as a Gaussian distribution.
source: We found that the world model on gravity was not a faithful replica of the physical laws, but instead encoded gravity's vertical direction as a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from psychophysics experiments

claim: The stochastic world model on gravity explains the illusion that taller objects are perceived as more likely to fall.
source: The world model with this stochastic feature fit nicely with participants' subjective sense of objects' stability and explained the illusion that taller objects are perceived as more likely to fall.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and comparison with human behavior

claim: The stochastic characteristic of the world model likely originated from experience-dependent comparisons between predictions formed by internal simulations and the realities observed in the external world.
source: Furthermore, a computational model with reinforcement learning revealed that the stochastic characteristic likely originated from experience-dependent comparisons between predictions formed by internal simulations and the realities observed in the external world
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with reinforcement learning

claim: The stochastic representation has an ecological advantage in balancing accuracy and speed for efficient stability inference.
source: which illustrated the ecological advantage of stochastic representation in balancing accuracy and speed for efficient stability inference.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling comparing efficiency of stochastic vs deterministic models

claim: The brain is proposed as a set of generative machines that actively predict future events of the ever-changing physical world through mental simulation with a priori knowledge.
source: Accordingly, our brain is proposed as a set of generative machines that actively predict future events of the ever-changing physical world through mental simulation with a priori knowledge acting upon the world (Battaglia et al., 2013; Hegarty, 2004; Huang and Rao, 2011; Tenenbaum et al., 2011; Ullman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical work (Battaglia et al., 2013; Hegarty, 2004; Huang and Rao, 2011; Tenenbaum et al., 2011; Ullman et al., 2017)

claim: A prevailing theory suggests that the world model in the brain accurately mirrors the physical laws of the world.
source: A prevailing theory suggests that the world model in the brain accurately mirrors the physical laws of the world (Allen et al., 2020; Battaglia et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical work (Allen et al., 2020; Battaglia et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2022)

claim: External noise, such as imperfect perception and assumed external forces, is introduced to explain the phenomenon that tall and thin objects are subjectively perceived as more unstable.
source: To explain the phenomenon that tall and thin objects are subjectively perceived as more unstable compared to short and fat ones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), external noise, such as imperfect perception and assumed external forces, is introduced to influence the output of the model.
evidence: Describes existing theoretical approaches in the literature

claim: When the brain actively transforms sensory data into cognitive understanding, these data can become distorted.
source: However, when the brain actively transforms sensory data into cognitive understanding, these data can become distorted (Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2019; Naselaris et al., 2011), hereby introducing uncertainty into the representation of gravity's direction.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2019; Naselaris et al., 2011)

claim: The variance of participants' confidence level about normal trajectory in θ angles ranged from 11.1 to 37.1.
source: This pattern was observed for all participants tested, with σ varying from 11.1 to 37.1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The pattern of Gaussian distribution remained unchanged with the addition of a wall on one side to block potential external disturbances from wind.
source: and remained unchanged with the addition of a wall on one side to block potential external disturbances from wind (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: In the upside-down condition, the confidence level decreased gradually as a function of θ with σ = 17.2.
source: We found that the confidence level also decreased gradually as a function of θ (Figure 1f, σ = 17.2; see Figure 1—figure supplement 5 for each participant)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: The σ in the upside-down condition was not significantly different from that in the environment with gravity pointing downward.
source: which was not significantly different from that in the environment with gravity pointing downward.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data

claim: 10 participants from Tsinghua University completed four runs of the behavioral experiment measuring their ability to detect the abnormality of stacks' collapse trajectories.
source: In this experiment, 10 participants (five females, age range: 21–28 y) from Tsinghua University were recruited to finish four runs of the behavioral experiment, which measured their ability to detect the abnormality of stacks' collapse trajectories.
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure and sample

claim: Another group of 11 participants from Tsinghua University completed a behavioral experiment for judging the stability of 60 stacks.
source: Another group of 11 participants (five females, age range: 21–32 y) from Tsinghua University completed a behavioral experiment for judging the stability of 60 stacks.
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure and sample

claim: One male participant was excluded from further analyses because his judgment showed an extremely weak correlation with the actual stability of stacks (rs < 0.30 for all experimental runs).
source: One male participant (age: 25 y) was excluded from further analyses because his judgment showed an extremely weak correlation with the actual stability of stacks (rs < 0.30 for all experimental runs) compared to the rest of the participants.
evidence: Describes data exclusion criteria and results

claim: The stacks used in the stability judgment experiment contained 26 unstable and 34 stable stacks.
source: The stacks contained 26 unstable and 34 stable stacks, which were randomly interleaved in each run.
evidence: Describes the experimental stimuli

claim: The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Tsinghua University (2022 no. 34).
source: The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Tsinghua University (2022 no. 34), and informed consent was obtained from all participants before the experiment.
evidence: States ethical approval information

claim: A deterministic model that combines gravity's veridical direction with external perturbations is theoretically equivalent to the stochastic model that represents gravity's direction in a Gaussian distribution.
source: A deterministic model that combines gravity's veridical direction with external perturbations, such as an external force or perceptual uncertainty (Allen et al., 2020; Battaglia et al., 2013; Lake et al., 2017; Smith and Vul, 2013), is theoretically equivalent to our stochastic model that represents gravity's direction in a Gaussian distribution
evidence: Theoretical comparison with citations to previous work (Allen et al., 2020; Battaglia et al., 2013; Lake et al., 2017; Smith and Vul, 2013)

claim: The cognitive impenetrability and self-consistency observed in this study favor the stochastic model over the deterministic one.
source: While the cognitive impenetrability and the self-consistency observed in this study, without resorting to an external perturbation, favor the stochastic model over the deterministic one
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings

claim: The stochastic feature of the world model may emerge as a biological agent interacts with the environment.
source: Therefore, the stochastic feature may emerge as a biological agent interacts with the environment, where the mismatches between external feedback from the environment and internal expectations from the world model are in turn used to fine-tune the world model (Friston et al., 2021; MacKay, 1956; Matsuo et al., 2022).
evidence: Theoretical proposal supported by citations (Friston et al., 2021; MacKay, 1956; Matsuo et al., 2022)

claim: The world model on gravity in humans may be constructed through the mechanism of predictive coding in a generative process.
source: Taken together, the finding from the RL framework implies that the world model on gravity in humans may also be constructed in the same way, possibly through the mechanism of the predictive coding in a generative process (Friston, 2018; Huang and Rao, 2011).
evidence: Speculative inference based on computational modeling results, supported by citations (Friston, 2018; Huang and Rao, 2011)

claim: The close link between human cognition and the physical world through interaction may shed light on the development of a new generation of AI with human-like intelligence.
source: Indeed, the close link between human cognition and the physical world through interaction may shed light on the development of a new generation of AI with human-like intelligence that can work flexibly in open-ended environments (Marcus, 2020; Marcus, 2018).
evidence: Speculative implication supported by citations (Marcus, 2020; Marcus, 2018)

claim: The stochastic world model on gravity provides an example of how a priori knowledge of the physical world is implemented in mind.
source: The stochastic world model on gravity provides an example of how a priori knowledge of the physical world is implemented in mind that helps humans operate flexibly in open-ended environments.
evidence: Summary claim based on the study's findings

claim: The world model on gravity is not a faithful replica of the physical world, but rather a stochastic model that captures the essence of the vertically downward direction of gravity as the maximum likelihood of a Gaussian distribution.
source: A series of psychophysics experiments showed that the world model on gravity is not a faithful replica of the physical world, but rather a stochastic model that captures the essence of the vertically downward direction of gravity as the maximum likelihood of a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The stochastic feature of the world model not only fits humans' stability inference behavior better than the deterministic model, but also provides new insight into the daily illusion that taller objects are perceived as more likely to collapse.
source: The stochastic feature of the world model not only fits humans' stability inference behavior better than the deterministic model, but also provides new insight into the daily illusion that taller objects are perceived as more likely to collapse.
evidence: Summary of findings comparing stochastic and deterministic models

claim: The stochastic feature well-balanced accuracy and speed to produce a unique ecological advantage for our survival in the physical world.
source: and well-balanced accuracy and speed to produce a unique ecological advantage for our survival in the physical world.
evidence: Summary of findings on efficiency analysis

claim: In the Noisy Newtonian Framework, intuitive physics is depicted as a combination of Newtonian physics and uncertainty generated by noise.
source: In the Noisy Newtonian Framework, intuitive physics is depicted as a combination of Newtonian physics and uncertainty generated by noise (Battaglia et al., 2013; Kubricht et al., 2017; Sanborn et al., 2013).
evidence: Describes existing theoretical framework with citations (Battaglia et al., 2013; Kubricht et al., 2017; Sanborn et al., 2013)

claim: The introduction of uncertainty helps to reconcile the misconception occurring under unfavorable conditions.
source: The introduction of uncertainty helps to reconcile the misconception occurring under unfavorable conditions, such as unfamiliar events or static scenes (Kaiser et al., 1992; Kaiser et al., 1986; Kim and Spelke, 1999; McCloskey, 1983; Smith and Vul, 2013)
evidence: Describes theoretical explanation with citations (Kaiser et al., 1992; Kaiser et al., 1986; Kim and Spelke, 1999; McCloskey, 1983; Smith and Vul, 2013)

claim: The noise in previous studies was thought to originate from sources such as perceptual uncertainty or external perturbations of forces, rather than from the intuitive physical engine itself.
source: The noise in previous studies was thought to originate from sources such as perceptual uncertainty or external perturbations of forces, rather than from the intuitive physical engine itself, which is thought to be a deterministic system.
evidence: Describes assumptions in previous theoretical work

claim: The inherent stochastic feature of gravity's direction did not need to rely on external noise to explain the illusory instability of taller objects.
source: The inherent stochastic feature of gravity's direction did not need to rely on external noise to explain the illusory instability of taller objects.
evidence: Inference based on the study's findings

claim: The stochastic nature of the world model on gravity was confirmed by the cognitive impenetrability of the Gaussian distribution of gravity's direction when gravity's direction in the physical world was reversed.
source: In addition, it was also confirmed by the cognitive impenetrability of the Gaussian distribution of gravity's direction when gravity's direction in the physical world was reversed (Pylyshyn, 1980).
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings, with citation (Pylyshyn, 1980)

claim: The RL framework was designed to simulate how an agent constructed the world model on gravity through agent-environment interactions.
source: In contrast to summarizing statistical patterns from experience (Bear et al., 2021; Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016), this framework was designed to simulate how an agent constructed the world model on gravity through agent-environment interactions.
evidence: Describes the computational modeling approach with citations (Bear et al., 2021; Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016)

claim: A Gaussian distribution of gravity's direction with the vertically downward direction as the maximum likelihood emerged after several generations of error minimization in the RL framework.
source: After several generations of error minimization, a Gaussian distribution of gravity's direction with the vertically downward direction as the maximum likelihood was similar to that observed in the human world model.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: When the physical worlds that the agent interacted with changed their appearance with stacks of different heights, the world models maintained their general patterns, but the stochastic representation of gravity's direction changed accordingly.
source: Interestingly, when the physical worlds that the agent interacted with changed their appearance with stacks of different heights, the world models maintained their general patterns, but the stochastic representation of gravity's direction changed accordingly.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: This finding supports the robustness of the active inference, which efficiently encodes critical features under different physical worlds.
source: This finding not only supports the robustness of the active inference (Hegarty, 2004; Ullman et al., 2017), which efficiently encodes critical features under different physical worlds
evidence: Inference based on computational modeling results, with citations (Hegarty, 2004; Ullman et al., 2017)

claim: The finding resonates with the idea that intelligence develops under the constraints of the physical world.
source: but also resonates with the idea that intelligence develops under the constraints of the physical world.
evidence: Inference based on computational modeling results

claim: The world model on gravity provides an example of the world model theory that emphasizes the predictive nature of generative neural networks implemented with a priori knowledge of the physical world.
source: Our world model on gravity provides an example of the world model theory that emphasizes the predictive nature of generative neural networks implemented with a priori knowledge of the physical world (Friston et al., 2021; Land, 2014; Matsuo et al., 2022).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation with citations (Friston et al., 2021; Land, 2014; Matsuo et al., 2022)

claim: Generative models equipped with the physics laws governing the physical world rely much less on experience than traditional discriminative neural networks.
source: In contrast to traditional discriminative neural networks that learn statistical patterns for stability from gigantic amounts of labeled stacks, generative models equipped with the physics laws governing the physical world rely much less on experience.
evidence: Theoretical comparison based on knowledge of neural network approaches

claim: The stochastic feature of the model further enhances the efficiency by balancing accuracy and speed, which improves our chances of better survival.
source: Importantly, the stochastic feature of the model further enhances the efficiency by balancing accuracy and speed, which improves our chances of better survival (Cosmides and Tooby, 1997) and adaptation to novel environments (e.g., astronauts in outer space; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Inference based on efficiency analysis, with citations (Cosmides and Tooby, 1997; Wang et al., 2022)
